modules.title: Programming and Software Engineering Foundations
modules.description: The C# and engineering basics every later lesson builds on.

lessons.title: What is software engineering?
lessons.summary: Coding is writing instructions a computer can run. Software engineering is building software that keeps working, keeps changing safely and can be looked after by a team for years. Learn the difference, why requirements come first, and why most of the cost arrives after launch.

lessons.title: What is a software system?
lessons.summary: A software system is a set of parts that work together to turn inputs into useful outputs for its users. Learn to see components, inputs and outputs, users and the boundary that separates what you build from what you depend on.

lessons.title: How a computer executes a program
lessons.summary: Follow a C# program from the text you type to electrical work in the CPU. Learn what the CPU and memory do, how the C# compiler produces IL, how the .NET runtime JIT-compiles it to machine code, and how processes and threads let many things run at once.

lessons.title: Variables, types, conditions, loops and functions in C#
lessons.summary: The five building blocks of every C# program. Store data in typed variables, make decisions with if and switch, repeat work with loops, and package steps into methods, then use them all to build a calculator.

lessons.title: Classes, objects, fields, properties and methods
lessons.summary: A class is a design; an object is one real thing built from it. Learn how fields store data, properties guard it, methods give it behaviour, and static members belong to the class itself.

lessons.title: Constructors and object initialization
lessons.summary: A constructor is the one moment you can insist an object is born valid. Learn parameterised and overloaded constructors, chaining, object initializers, required and init members, primary constructors, records and static factories, and when to use each.

lessons.title: Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism
lessons.summary: The four ideas behind object-oriented design, explained with a highway toll plaza. Hide data behind rules, hide complexity behind simple contracts, share behaviour through inheritance, and let one call do the right thing for many types.

lessons.title: Interfaces and abstract classes
lessons.summary: An interface is a promise of what a class can do; an abstract class is a half-built class that others finish. Learn both from scratch in C#, including default interface methods, a first look at static abstract members, and a simple way to choose between them.

lessons.title: Value types, reference types and memory basics
lessons.summary: Why changing one variable sometimes changes another. Learn how value types are copied and reference types are shared, where the stack and heap fit in, what boxing costs, how to choose struct or class, and how the garbage collector cleans up.

lessons.title: Exceptions and error handling
lessons.summary: How C# reports that something went wrong. Learn try, catch and finally, which built-in exceptions to throw, when a custom exception helps, and when you should not throw at all, then build a bank account that validates every operation.

lessons.title: Collections, generics and common data structures
lessons.summary: Learn which container to put your data in. List, Dictionary, HashSet, Queue and Stack each answer a different question quickly; generics make them type-safe; LINQ lets you ask questions of them in one readable line.

lessons.title: Big O notation, time and space complexity
lessons.summary: Big O describes how the work your code does grows as the data grows. Learn to read it from code, estimate what it means in seconds, and spot the hidden quadratic loops that make systems fall over at scale.

lessons.title: Basic algorithms relevant to software design
lessons.summary: The handful of algorithms that keep showing up in real business software, not just in puzzles. Binary search, sorting with comparers, hashing and equality, recursion over trees, and the two-pointer technique, each with a realistic C# use and its failure modes.

lessons.title: Unit testing and debugging fundamentals
lessons.summary: How professionals know their code works and find out why it doesn't. Write xUnit tests with arrange-act-assert, replace slow or unpredictable parts with test doubles, and track down bugs with breakpoints instead of guesswork.

lessons.title: Git, branches, commits and code reviews
lessons.summary: How teams change the same code without losing work. Learn what a commit really is, how branches, merges and rebases work, how pull requests and code reviews keep quality high, and build a small commit-message linter in C#.

modules.title: Understanding Applications and Architecture
modules.description: What architecture is, the main styles, and how to choose between them.

lessons.title: What is software architecture?
topics: decisions that are hard to change
lessons.summary: Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to change later. Learn to spot those decisions, describe the qualities a system must have (speed, availability, security and more) as measurable targets, and understand what an architect actually does.

lessons.title: What is system design?
lessons.summary: A gentle introduction to system design — the common building blocks, how data flows between them, why scale changes everything, and the trade-offs behind each step — walked through by growing a meal-delivery app from one server to a scaled system.

lessons.title: HLD versus LLD
lessons.summary: What high-level design (HLD) and low-level design (LLD) each decide, the artefacts each produces, and how they connect — shown by designing one feature, a construction site-inspection request, at both levels and in C#.

lessons.title: Functional and non-functional requirements
lessons.summary: What a system must do (functional requirements) versus how well it must do it (non-functional requirements), the common quality attributes, how to turn vague wishes into measurable targets, and how to write user stories with testable acceptance criteria — with C# that checks both.

lessons.title: Business requirements and technical constraints
lessons.summary: Business goals tell you why a system exists, and constraints tell you which designs are not allowed. Learn to collect budget, team, compliance, legacy, deadline and data-residency constraints, turn them into architecture decisions, and enforce them in ASP.NET Core code.

lessons.title: Monolithic architecture
lessons.summary: A monolith is one application built, tested and deployed as a single unit. Learn why it is usually the right first architecture, how it fails when it grows without structure, and how to scale it a long way before splitting it up.

lessons.title: Layered architecture
lessons.summary: Split an application into stacked layers (presentation, business, data) where each layer only depends on the ones below it. Learn strict versus relaxed layering, the sinkhole anti-pattern, and how a layered EMS compares with a plain monolith and a modular monolith.

lessons.title: Client-server architecture
lessons.summary: In client-server architecture, clients send requests and servers send responses. Learn the request/response cycle, the difference between thin and thick clients, why servers should be stateless, and how to build clients that cope with timeouts and retries.

lessons.title: Three-tier and n-tier architecture
lessons.summary: Tiers are the physical places where code runs, and layers are how code is organised. Learn the classic three-tier design (presentation, application, data), how n-tier adds more, and why every extra network hop costs latency, availability and money.

lessons.title: Modular monolith architecture
lessons.summary: Build one deployable application that is split inside into modules with hard boundaries, small public contracts and private internals, and enforce those boundaries with automated architecture tests.

lessons.title: Service-oriented architecture
lessons.summary: Organise an enterprise's systems as reusable business services that talk through formal contracts, often via an enterprise service bus that routes and transforms messages, and learn how this differs from microservices.

lessons.title: Microservices architecture
lessons.summary: Split a product into small services that each own their data and can be deployed on their own, and learn exactly what that costs, how to keep services independent, and when not to do it.

lessons.title: Event-driven architecture
lessons.summary: Build systems where components announce facts as events and others react on their own, and learn the difference between event notification and event-carried state transfer, plus how to live with eventual consistency, duplicates and ordering.

lessons.title: Hexagonal architecture
lessons.summary: Put the business logic in the middle, let it talk to the outside world only through interfaces it defines (ports), and plug in technology-specific adapters for HTTP, databases, email and tests.

lessons.title: Clean Architecture and Onion Architecture
lessons.summary: Organise code in rings with business entities at the centre and frameworks at the edge, follow the dependency rule (source code points only inward), and lay it out as Domain, Application, Infrastructure and API projects in .NET.

lessons.title: Vertical Slice Architecture
lessons.summary: Organise code by feature instead of by technical layer, so everything one use case needs (endpoint, validation, handler, data access) lives together and changes together.

lessons.title: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
lessons.summary: Write down each important architecture decision as a short, numbered, immutable document with its context, the decision and its consequences, so future engineers know why the system looks the way it does.

lessons.title: Coupling, cohesion, modularity and separation of concerns
lessons.summary: Learn to see how strongly parts of a system depend on each other (coupling) and how well each part sticks to one job (cohesion), and measure both with afferent/efferent coupling, instability and LCOM in C#.

modules.title: C# and ASP.NET Core Application Architecture
modules.description: How a real ASP.NET Core app is put together, end to end.

lessons.title: How an ASP.NET Core application starts
lessons.summary: What really happens between `dotnet run` and the first request — Program.cs, WebApplication.CreateBuilder, the host, the two phases (register services, then build the pipeline) and environments.

lessons.title: HTTP request and response lifecycle
lessons.summary: Follow one HTTP request end to end — browser, TCP and TLS, Kestrel, middleware, routing, endpoint, service, repository, PostgreSQL and back — with a sequence diagram and realistic timing estimates for each hop.

lessons.title: Kestrel, middleware, routing, controllers and minimal APIs
lessons.summary: How Kestrel turns bytes into an HttpContext, how the middleware pipeline wraps every request (and why its order matters), how routing picks an endpoint, and when to write that endpoint as a controller action or a minimal API.

lessons.title: Dependency injection
lessons.summary: Why classes should receive their dependencies instead of creating them, and how ASP.NET Core's built-in container does it — IServiceCollection, constructor injection, registering interfaces, multiple and keyed implementations, and validation at startup.

lessons.title: Singleton, scoped and transient services
lessons.summary: How long each service instance lives — singleton, scoped and transient — what a scope is, how disposal works, how captive dependencies break apps, how scope validation catches them, why DbContext is scoped, and how background services use IServiceScopeFactory correctly.

lessons.title: Controllers, services, repositories and domain models
lessons.summary: What each layer of a typical ASP.NET Core app is responsible for (controller, service, repository, domain model), which way the dependencies must point, and how to tell when you have more layers than the problem needs.

lessons.title: DTOs, entities, mapping and validation
lessons.summary: Why the objects you accept and return over HTTP should be different from the objects you store, how to map between them without losing your mind, and how to validate input so bad requests become clear 400 responses in the standard ProblemDetails format.

lessons.title: Configuration, environment variables and secrets
lessons.summary: Where settings come from and who wins — appsettings files, environment variables, command line, user secrets and Azure Key Vault — and how to turn them into typed, validated options (IOptions, IOptionsSnapshot, IOptionsMonitor) that fail fast at startup and never leak secrets.

lessons.title: Authentication and authorization
lessons.summary: How ASP.NET Core decides who is calling (cookies, JWT bearer tokens, claims) and what they may do (roles, policies, requirements and handlers, resource-based checks), plus where ASP.NET Core Identity fits.

lessons.title: Filters, middleware and exception handling
lessons.summary: Where cross-cutting code belongs (middleware, MVC filters or endpoint filters), and how to build one global error pipeline with IExceptionHandler and ProblemDetails that maps domain exceptions to the right HTTP status codes without leaking internals.

lessons.title: Logging and observability
lessons.summary: Use ILogger the way production teams do: structured messages with named properties, scopes that stamp every line with a correlation id, the right level for each event, and a clear list of what must never reach a log file.

lessons.title: Asynchronous programming with async/await
lessons.summary: What really happens when you write await, why a web server with 20 threads can serve 5,000 waiting requests, how sync-over-async starves the thread pool, and the handful of rules (async all the way, no async void, WhenAll for fan-out, ValueTask only on hot paths) that keep ASP.NET Core services fast.

lessons.title: Cancellation tokens and request cancellation
lessons.summary: How .NET stops work that nobody needs any more: CancellationToken and CancellationTokenSource, request aborts, timeouts, linked tokens, checking for cancellation in loops and database calls, and knowing when not to cancel.

lessons.title: Background services and hosted workers
lessons.summary: Run work outside the request: BackgroundService and IHostedService, in-process queues with System.Threading.Channels, scoped services inside singleton workers, PeriodicTimer schedules, failure handling and graceful shutdown, and when to reach for a durable queue instead.

lessons.title: API versioning, pagination, filtering and sorting
lessons.summary: Shape list endpoints that stay fast and predictable at 200 rows or 2 million: bounded page sizes, keyset cursors, allow-listed filters and sorts, one response envelope, and a versioning policy that lets old clients keep working.

lessons.title: REST API design and HTTP status codes
lessons.summary: Design an HTTP API that other developers can guess: nouns for resources, verbs from HTTP, the right status code for every outcome, and one consistent error body. Includes the module's end-to-end employee management API.

lessons.title: API documentation with OpenAPI
lessons.summary: Make the employee API describe itself: generate an OpenAPI document with ASP.NET Core 10's built-in support, enrich it with XML comments and examples, browse it in Swagger UI or Scalar, and publish separate documents per API version.

lessons.title: Caching in ASP.NET Core
lessons.summary: Make the employee API fast without serving wrong data: IMemoryCache, IDistributedCache and HybridCache for data, output caching for whole responses, Cache-Control and ETags for browsers and CDNs, and a deliberate invalidation plan for every cached thing.

lessons.title: Health checks and graceful shutdown
lessons.summary: Tell the platform the truth about your service: liveness, readiness and startup health checks in ASP.NET Core, and a shutdown sequence that drains traffic, finishes in-flight work and exits before the kill signal. Ends with the module's complete employee management API project.

modules.title: SOLID Principles and Clean Code
modules.description: Principles that keep code easy to change, and when they go too far.

lessons.title: Single Responsibility Principle
lessons.summary: Group code by who asks for changes to it. A class should have one reason to change, which in practice means it serves one group of people (one actor), so a change for finance never breaks a report for the client.

lessons.title: Open/Closed Principle
lessons.summary: Design the parts of your code that change often so that new behaviour arrives as new code or new data, not as edits to code that already works — and only for the changes you can actually predict.

lessons.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
lessons.summary: A subtype must keep every promise its base type makes, so code written against the base type keeps working when handed any subtype — no type checks, no surprise exceptions, no broken assumptions.

lessons.title: Interface Segregation Principle
lessons.summary: Give each client a small interface that contains only what it uses, so a change for one client never forces work on another — and know when splitting goes too far.

lessons.title: Dependency Inversion Principle
lessons.summary: Make business rules own the interfaces they need, and make databases, HTTP clients and clocks plug into them — so the important code never depends on the replaceable code.

lessons.title: DRY, KISS and YAGNI
lessons.summary: Keep each piece of business knowledge in one place (DRY), choose the simplest design that works (KISS), and don't build features before they're needed (YAGNI) — and learn where each rule stops helping.

lessons.title: Code smells and technical debt
lessons.summary: Learn to recognise the fourteen most common code smells, apply the matching refactoring in small safe steps, and manage technical debt deliberately using the debt quadrant and change hotspots.

lessons.title: Composition versus inheritance
lessons.summary: Prefer building behaviour from small parts you hold (composition) over inheriting it from a parent class, understand the fragile base class problem, and recognise the cases where inheritance is still the right tool.

lessons.title: Dependency injection versus service locator
lessons.summary: Why asking a global container for what you need ("service locator") hides dependencies and moves failures to runtime, how constructor injection fixes it, and the few places in ASP.NET Core where resolving from IServiceProvider is the right call.

lessons.title: Refactoring legacy code
lessons.summary: How to change code that has no tests without breaking it — pin its current behaviour with characterization tests, open seams to break dependencies, add features with sprout and wrap, and replace old logic gradually with a code-level strangler.

lessons.title: Designing for testability
lessons.summary: Design code so that tests are easy to write — keep decisions in pure functions, push I/O to a thin shell, inject time with TimeProvider, fake HTTP with a stub handler, and pick the right kind of test double for each job.

lessons.title: Identifying overengineering and underengineering
lessons.summary: How to tell when a design is doing too much or too little — the real cost of abstractions, the rule of three, reversible versus irreversible decisions, and the places (money, data, security, contracts) where cutting corners is never "simple".

modules.title: UML and Visual Design
modules.description: Read and draw the diagrams engineers actually use.

lessons.title: UML fundamentals
lessons.summary: What UML is, the three families of diagrams, when a diagram saves time and when it wastes it, sketch versus blueprint, and how to write diagrams as text with Mermaid so they live next to your code.

lessons.title: Class diagrams
lessons.summary: Read and draw UML class diagrams with confidence. Every relationship arrow, multiplicity and visibility symbol, what each one means in C#, and how to write them in Mermaid so your diagrams live next to your code.

lessons.title: Object diagrams
lessons.summary: Draw snapshots of real objects and the links between them at one moment in time. Use them to explain tricky structures, find aliasing bugs, check examples against a class diagram, and see exactly what a C# object graph looks like in memory.

lessons.title: Sequence diagrams
lessons.summary: Draw who talks to whom, in what order. Lifelines, synchronous and asynchronous messages, activation bars and the alt/opt/loop/par fragments, written in Mermaid and mapped to C#. Includes a full HTTP request travelling through ASP.NET Core.

lessons.title: Activity diagrams
lessons.summary: Draw and read UML activity diagrams for business workflows. Actions, decisions and merges, forks and joins for parallel work, swimlanes for "who does what", how to write them as Mermaid flowcharts, and how each element maps to C# async code.

lessons.title: State machine diagrams
lessons.summary: Model an object's lifecycle with UML state machine diagrams. States, events, transitions, guards, entry and exit actions, composite states and pseudo-states, how to write them in Mermaid stateDiagram-v2, and how to turn them into a safe, testable C# state machine.

lessons.title: Component diagrams
lessons.summary: Draw UML component diagrams that show the replaceable parts of a system, the interfaces each part provides and requires, and how they connect. Learn to write them in Mermaid, and map each component to a .NET project, a public contract and a DI registration that the compiler and tests can enforce.

lessons.title: Deployment diagrams
lessons.summary: Draw UML deployment diagrams that show where software physically runs. Nodes, execution environments, artifacts, communication paths and deployment specifications, written in Mermaid, and mapped to IIS, virtual machines, containers and the configuration, health checks and hosting code an ASP.NET Core app needs on each.

lessons.title: Entity-relationship diagrams
lessons.summary: Read and draw entity-relationship diagrams in crow's foot notation. Entities, attributes, keys, cardinality and optionality, how to write them in Mermaid erDiagram syntax, and exactly how each line becomes PostgreSQL tables, foreign keys and constraints.

lessons.title: C4 architecture model
lessons.summary: The C4 model gives you four zoom levels for software architecture diagrams (system context, container, component and code), a small notation, and a clear idea of who each diagram is for. Learn the abstractions, the notation rules, the audiences, and how to keep C4 diagrams as code.

lessons.title: Context, container, component and code-level views
lessons.summary: A complete worked C4 example for a realistic construction progress-reporting system. Build the system context, container, component and code views one zoom at a time as Mermaid flowcharts, explain every box and arrow, and see how the lowest view becomes real ASP.NET Core code.

lessons.title: Reading and creating architecture diagrams
lessons.summary: A repeatable method for reading any architecture diagram, and for drawing ones other people can read. Legends, choosing the level of detail, arrow semantics, the ten most common diagram mistakes, and a checklist for reviewing a diagram in a pull request, with a C# linter that automates the mechanical checks.

lessons.title: Mapping diagrams to code and database structures
lessons.summary: Turn class diagrams into C# and ER diagrams into PostgreSQL tables, and go back the other way, without losing meaning. Every relationship, multiplicity and key becomes a specific line of code or a constraint; the mismatches between objects and tables are named and handled; and round-trip checks catch drift between diagram, code and schema.

modules.title: Design Patterns — The Complete Catalogue
modules.description: Every GoF pattern plus the enterprise patterns used in modern .NET.

lessons.title: What design patterns are and how to learn them
lessons.summary: A design pattern is a named, proven answer to a problem that keeps coming back. Learn where the catalogue came from, its three families, how to read any pattern, and how to spot patterns already inside .NET and ASP.NET Core.

lessons.title: Singleton
lessons.summary: Make sure only one instance of a class exists and everyone shares it. Learn the classic C# versions, why they hurt testing, and why a DI singleton lifetime is the modern answer, including the captive-dependency trap.

lessons.title: Factory Method
lessons.summary: Let a subclass (or a registered function) decide which concrete class to create, so the code that uses the object never writes `new ConcreteThing()`. Learn the GoF form, its modern .NET variants, and when a plain constructor is better.

lessons.title: Abstract Factory
lessons.summary: One object creates a whole family of related objects (a payment provider's charge client, refund client and webhook verifier) so the pieces always match. Learn when a family really exists, how DI changes the pattern, and the real cost of adding a new product.

lessons.title: Builder
lessons.summary: Build a complicated object step by step, check it once at the end, and hand back a finished, valid result. Learn the GoF Builder with a Director, the fluent builder you meet in ASP.NET Core, and when C# records and `required` make a builder unnecessary.

lessons.title: Prototype
lessons.summary: Make new objects by copying a ready-made, fully configured example instead of building each one from scratch, and learn exactly what "copy" means for references, lists and records in C#.

lessons.title: Object Pool
lessons.summary: Reuse expensive objects (large buffers, connections, handlers) instead of creating and destroying them on every request, using ArrayPool, Microsoft.Extensions.ObjectPool, DbContext pooling and IHttpClientFactory, and learn when pooling makes things worse.

lessons.title: Adapter
lessons.summary: Wrap a third-party SDK or legacy service behind an interface your application owns, so the rest of your code never sees the vendor's formats, error codes or quirks, and switching vendors means writing one new class.

lessons.title: Decorator
lessons.summary: Add behaviour such as caching, logging and retries around an object by wrapping it in another object with the same interface, without changing the original class or exploding into subclasses, and wire the wrappers up in ASP.NET Core DI without extra libraries.

lessons.title: Facade
lessons.summary: Give a complicated set of classes one simple front door. Callers make a single call, and the facade coordinates the subsystems in the right order, while the subsystems stay available for anyone who needs the detail.

lessons.title: Proxy
lessons.summary: Put a stand-in object in front of the real one, with the same interface, so you can delay, guard, cache, log or forward calls to it without changing the caller or the real object.

lessons.title: Composite
lessons.summary: Treat a single item and a group of items through the same interface, so code can total, render or search a whole tree (folders, org charts, BOQ cost breakdowns, menus) without asking "is this a leaf or a group?".

lessons.title: Bridge
lessons.summary: When a concept varies in two independent ways (report type and export format, notification type and channel), split it into two hierarchies joined by a reference, so you write M + N classes instead of M × N.

lessons.title: Flyweight
lessons.summary: When you have huge numbers of similar objects, share the heavy, unchanging part (icon, style, glyph shape) between all of them and keep only the small, varying part (position, status) per object, cutting memory by orders of magnitude.

lessons.title: Strategy
lessons.summary: Put each way of doing a job (each pricing rule, each payment provider) behind one interface, so you can add or swap them without editing the code that uses them.

lessons.title: Observer
lessons.summary: Let one object announce "something happened" while any number of other objects react, without the announcer knowing who they are. Covers C# events, IObservable/IObserver, leaks from forgotten subscriptions, in-process domain events and Channels.

lessons.title: Command
lessons.summary: Turn a request ("change this quantity", "approve this bill") into an object you can store, queue, retry, log and undo. Covers undo/redo, command queues, background jobs, CQRS commands and command handlers in ASP.NET Core.

lessons.title: State
lessons.summary: Let an object change its behaviour when its status changes, without a switch in every method. Covers order lifecycles and approval workflows, state classes vs transition tables, persisting state, and guarding against invalid or racing transitions.

lessons.title: Template Method
lessons.summary: Fix the order of steps in a base class and let subclasses fill in only the steps that differ. Covers report pipelines, hooks, BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync as a real example, and when composition with Strategy is the better choice.

lessons.title: Chain of Responsibility
lessons.summary: Pass a request along a line of handlers until one deals with it, or let each handler do its part and pass it on. Covers amount-based approval chains, ASP.NET Core middleware, HttpClient DelegatingHandler chains and validation chains.

lessons.title: Mediator
lessons.summary: Stop objects talking to each other directly. Route their conversations through one coordinator, either a classic GoF mediator for UI-style collaboration or an in-process request dispatcher with pipeline behaviours.

lessons.title: Iterator
lessons.summary: Walk through the items of any collection, tree, file or database result one at a time, without knowing how it's stored, using IEnumerable, yield return and IAsyncEnumerable to stream data lazily instead of loading it all.

lessons.title: Memento
lessons.summary: Capture an object's state in a sealed snapshot so you can restore it later (undo, rollback, saved drafts) without exposing the object's internals to the code that stores the snapshot.

lessons.title: Visitor
lessons.summary: Add new operations (totals, exports, validation, rewriting) to a fixed family of node types without editing those types, using double dispatch, and know when a C# pattern-matching switch is the simpler choice.

lessons.title: Interpreter
lessons.summary: Represent a small language (such as eligibility rules like amount > 5000 AND region = 'NORTH') as a grammar and a tree of node objects, parse text into that tree, then evaluate it directly or compile it with System.Linq.Expressions. Also learn when to use a parser library or an existing engine instead.

lessons.title: Specification
lessons.summary: Turn each business rule ("turnover at least ₹50 crore", "not debarred") into a small named object that can be combined with And, Or and Not, checked against one object in memory, or translated into a database query.

lessons.title: Repository and Unit of Work, including their limitations
lessons.summary: A repository makes stored objects look like an in-memory collection; a unit of work saves every change from one business operation together or not at all. Learn how they work, why EF Core's DbContext already gives you both, and when a repository still earns its place.

lessons.title: Null Object
lessons.summary: Replace "is it null?" checks with an object that safely does nothing (a do-nothing SMS sender, NullLogger, an "unregistered vendor"), and learn when absence should instead be an Option, an exception, or a startup error.

lessons.title: Dependency Injection as a pattern
lessons.summary: Objects receive the things they need instead of creating them. Learn the injection styles, the composition root, pure DI without a container, lifetimes and the captive-dependency bug, keyed services, and decorators in Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.

lessons.title: Options pattern and Result pattern
lessons.summary: Two small patterns that make services honest. Options turns configuration into typed, validated objects (IOptions, IOptionsSnapshot, IOptionsMonitor, ValidateOnStart). Result makes expected failures part of a method's return type instead of hidden exceptions, and maps them cleanly to ProblemDetails.

lessons.title: Pipeline and middleware pattern
lessons.summary: Build processing as a line of small, independent steps. Learn pipes and filters, build ASP.NET Core's middleware pipeline yourself from Func<RequestDelegate, RequestDelegate>, get middleware order right, and run data-processing pipelines with backpressure using System.Threading.Channels.

lessons.title: Choosing between similar patterns
lessons.summary: Many design patterns share the same class diagram and differ only in intent. Learn the questions that tell them apart — what varies, who chooses, does the interface change, how many objects are wrapped — and pick the right one for the problem in front of you.

lessons.title: Anti-patterns
lessons.summary: Fourteen common "solutions" that look reasonable and then cost you for years — god objects, magic numbers, singleton abuse, service locators, distributed monoliths and more — with the symptom to spot, the cause, the fix, and a C# example of each.

modules.title: Object-Oriented LLD Fundamentals
modules.description: How to turn requirements into classes that are easy to change and test.

lessons.title: Identifying classes and responsibilities
lessons.summary: Turn a written requirement into a small set of classes, decide which class should do which job, and use the GRASP principles to defend those decisions in a design review or interview.

lessons.title: Identifying entities, value objects and services
lessons.summary: Learn to sort every concept in a model into one of three roles (things with identity, values defined by their content, and stateless operations) and implement each correctly in C#.

lessons.title: Modeling object relationships
lessons.summary: Decide how your classes connect (which ones know about which, how many of each, and in which direction), then turn those decisions into C# fields, parameters and collections that stay consistent.

lessons.title: Association, aggregation and composition
lessons.summary: Tell apart "knows about", "has" and "owns" between objects, and turn each into the right C# code for creation, copying, deletion and disposal, plus the matching database rules.

lessons.title: Designing interfaces and abstractions
lessons.summary: Design interfaces from what the caller needs, write down their contracts, keep infrastructure details from leaking through them, and know when not to add an interface at all.

lessons.title: Encapsulation and invariant protection
lessons.summary: Decide which rules must always be true for an object, then use constructors, guard clauses, private setters and read-only views so no caller (not even a `with` expression or a race condition) can break them.

lessons.title: Object lifecycle and state management
lessons.summary: Give every important object a clear birth (a valid starting state), a small set of allowed moves between states, and a clean ending (disposal or a terminal state), so it can never end up half-paid, double-cancelled or leaking resources.

lessons.title: Domain modeling
lessons.summary: Turn the words and rules of a business into classes that speak the same language, keep their own rules, and protect themselves — so the code changes in the same places the business changes.

lessons.title: Validation and business rules
lessons.summary: Check that a request is well-formed at the edge, check facts that need data in the application layer, and enforce business rules inside the domain — each in one place, with errors a client can act on.

lessons.title: Error handling and domain exceptions
lessons.summary: Sort failures into bugs, business refusals and infrastructure faults; model business refusals as specific domain exceptions or results with stable codes; and translate everything to HTTP in one place without leaking internals.

lessons.title: Immutable objects
lessons.summary: Objects that never change after creation are safe to share, cache and pass between threads. Learn records, init, with-expressions, immutable collections and the traps — shallow immutability, with bypassing validation, and broken equality.

lessons.title: Equality and identity
lessons.summary: Decide what "the same" means for each type — same object, same identity, or same value — and implement Equals, GetHashCode, records and comparers so collections, caches and deduplication behave correctly.

lessons.title: Testable object design
lessons.summary: Design classes whose hidden inputs (time, randomness, I/O) come in through seams, so business rules can be tested quickly and deterministically with simple hand-written fakes.

lessons.title: Dependency graphs and circular dependencies
lessons.summary: See your code as a directed graph of "uses" arrows, find the cycles that make modules impossible to change or test alone, and break them with dependency inversion, extraction, events or a higher-level coordinator.

lessons.title: Refactoring large classes
lessons.summary: Take a 2,000-line class apart safely — find its hidden responsibilities from field usage and change history, pin its behaviour with characterization tests, then extract classes in small, reversible steps behind a stable facade.

lessons.title: Designing extensible business workflows
lessons.summary: Separate the four things that change in a business process — rules, routing, lifecycle states and steps — and give each its own extension point, using leave approval and procurement as worked examples.

modules.title: Advanced LLD and Domain-Driven Design
modules.description: Tactical and strategic DDD for real business systems.

lessons.title: Entities and value objects in DDD
lessons.summary: Build the two smallest DDD building blocks properly in C# 14 — entities that keep their identity while they change, and immutable, self-validating value objects such as Money, Quantity, Address and GSTIN — using a procurement domain.

lessons.title: Aggregates and aggregate roots
lessons.summary: Draw the boundary around the objects that must change together (an aggregate), expose it through one entry point (the aggregate root), keep it small, reference other aggregates by id, and protect it from concurrent edits with a version number.

lessons.title: Repositories and domain services
lessons.summary: Give every aggregate one repository that behaves like an in-memory collection, keep the domain unaware of how it is stored (persistence ignorance), and put business logic that belongs to no single entity into small, stateless domain services.

lessons.title: Domain events
lessons.summary: Let aggregates record "something important happened" as small immutable facts, collect them when you save, dispatch them to in-process handlers after the commit, and publish only selected, versioned integration events to other systems through an outbox.

lessons.title: Application services
lessons.summary: Write each use case as a thin application service that checks permissions, loads aggregates, calls the domain, commits one transaction and returns a DTO, while every business rule stays in the domain.

lessons.title: Bounded contexts and ubiquitous language
lessons.summary: Draw a line around each part of the business where words have one clear meaning (a bounded context), name the relationships between those parts (a context map), and protect your model from someone else's with a translation layer (an anti-corruption layer).

lessons.title: Strategic and tactical DDD
lessons.summary: Decide where the business actually makes its money (the core subdomain), spend your best design effort there, buy or keep simple everything else, and know when Domain-Driven Design is more ceremony than a problem deserves.

lessons.title: Transaction boundaries and aggregate consistency
lessons.summary: Change one aggregate per transaction, let other aggregates catch up through events (eventual consistency), coordinate multi-step workflows with an explicit process manager even inside a monolith, and protect each aggregate with a version number and a retry on conflict.

lessons.title: CQRS fundamentals
lessons.summary: Split the code that changes data (commands) from the code that reads it (queries), give reads their own simple, fast shape (a read model), and know when that split pays for itself and when a single model is enough.

lessons.title: Domain versus infrastructure dependencies
lessons.summary: Keep business rules free of databases, HTTP clients and frameworks: the domain declares the interfaces it needs (ports), infrastructure implements them (adapters), every dependency points inward, and tests swap in simple hand-written fakes.

lessons.title: Domain-driven modular monoliths
lessons.summary: Build one deployable ASP.NET Core application that is split inside into independent modules, one per bounded context, that talk only through small public APIs and events, never through each other's tables.

lessons.title: Clean Architecture in ASP.NET Core
lessons.summary: Lay out an ASP.NET Core solution as Domain, Application, Infrastructure and Web projects, point every reference inward, put use cases in handlers, and know exactly which file goes where, and when the whole thing is more than your project needs.

lessons.title: Vertical Slice Architecture in practice
lessons.summary: Organise a real ASP.NET Core system by feature: one slice per endpoint holding its request, validation, handler and mapping, a rich domain model that slices share, a deliberately small shared kernel, ordered cross-cutting behaviours, and a clear way to combine slices with Clean Architecture.

lessons.title: Event sourcing fundamentals and trade-offs
lessons.summary: Store every change as an immutable event in an append-only stream, rebuild current state by replaying it, feed read models from the same events, and understand the real costs: versioning, snapshots, projections, privacy, and when plain state tables are the better choice.

lessons.title: Project: Order management domain
lessons.summary: Build a small but honest order management domain (products, customers, orders, payments and inventory reservations) with explicit domain rules, status transitions, transaction boundaries and tests, then defend every boundary you drew.

modules.title: Database Design and Data Modeling
modules.description: Model, index, and scale relational data in PostgreSQL.

lessons.title: Relational database fundamentals
lessons.summary: Tables, rows, columns, keys and constraints: how a relational database turns business rules into guarantees, with PostgreSQL 17 DDL, the right data types, NULL semantics and the first joins.

lessons.title: One-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many
lessons.summary: How to model the three relationship shapes in PostgreSQL: where the foreign key lives, when a junction table is needed, how to carry attributes on a relationship, self-referencing hierarchies, and the queries each shape makes easy or hard.

lessons.title: Normalization and denormalization
lessons.summary: Normalization stores each fact exactly once so that updates cannot contradict each other. Learn functional dependencies, 1NF to 3NF and BCNF on a real procurement spreadsheet, then learn when and how to denormalize on purpose without letting copies drift.

lessons.title: Indexes, composite indexes, B-tree and hash
lessons.summary: An index is a sorted shortcut to rows, paid for on every write. Learn how PostgreSQL 17 B-tree, hash, GIN and BRIN indexes work, how to order composite index columns, when covering and partial indexes win, and how to count the write cost before you add one more index.

lessons.title: Query planning and EXPLAIN ANALYZE
lessons.summary: PostgreSQL decides how to run your query by estimating costs from statistics. Learn to read EXPLAIN ANALYZE output node by node, recognise scan types and join algorithms, spot the misestimates that cause most slow plans, and apply the fixes that actually work.

lessons.title: Transactions and ACID
lessons.summary: A transaction is an all-or-nothing envelope around several SQL statements. Learn what atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability really promise in PostgreSQL 17, how the write-ahead log keeps those promises, and how to use transactions correctly from ASP.NET Core without holding them open too long.

lessons.title: Isolation levels and anomalies
lessons.summary: PostgreSQL offers three real isolation levels. This lesson shows, with step-by-step interleavings, exactly which anomalies each one allows (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, write skew), how Serializable detects conflicts, and how to write the retry loop every Serializable application needs.

lessons.title: Deadlocks, optimistic and pessimistic locking
lessons.summary: When two requests change the same row at the same moment, someone has to wait, retry or lose. Learn PostgreSQL row and table locks, SELECT FOR UPDATE, NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED, optimistic concurrency with a version column or xmin, how deadlocks form and how to prevent them, and how to retry safely from ASP.NET Core.

lessons.title: Database connection pooling
lessons.summary: Opening a PostgreSQL connection is expensive and each one costs the server a process. Learn how Npgsql's pool works, size pools with Little's Law, fit many app instances under max_connections, choose PgBouncer session or transaction mode, and recognise and fix pool exhaustion.

lessons.title: Migrations and schema evolution
lessons.summary: How to change a live PostgreSQL schema without downtime — versioned migrations, which ALTER TABLE statements lock or rewrite, the expand/contract sequence across deploys, and safe batched backfills in C#.

lessons.title: N+1 query problems and EF Core performance
lessons.summary: Why a page that loads 50 rows can fire 51 queries, how to see it, and the EF Core tools that fix it — Include, projections, split queries, AsNoTracking and compiled queries — with the trade-offs of each.

lessons.title: Offset versus keyset pagination
lessons.summary: Why "page 400" gets slower and skips rows, how keyset (cursor) pagination fixes both with a stable sort key and a tie-breaker, and how to encode cursors safely in C#.

lessons.title: PostgreSQL JSONB
lessons.summary: How PostgreSQL stores and queries JSON documents with jsonb — the operators, SQL/JSON path, GIN and expression indexes — and a practical rule for when a field belongs in a column instead.

lessons.title: Read replicas and replication lag
lessons.summary: How PostgreSQL streaming replication copies writes to read replicas, why replicas lag, which consistency guarantees break, and how to route reads in ASP.NET Core so users always see their own writes.

lessons.title: Partitioning and sharding
lessons.summary: How PostgreSQL declarative range, list and hash partitioning splits one big table, how partition pruning and retention work, and how sharding spreads data across servers — choosing a shard key, logical shards, routing in C#, and Citus-style distribution.

lessons.title: Relational versus document and other databases
lessons.summary: How relational, document, key-value, wide-column, graph, time-series and search databases differ, which access patterns each serves best, how far PostgreSQL alone can go, and how to keep several stores consistent when you do need them.

modules.title: APIs and Communication
modules.description: How services talk, and how to keep those conversations safe under failure.

lessons.title: HTTP fundamentals
lessons.summary: Learn what an HTTP request really carries, which methods are safe to retry, how status codes and caching headers let clients and CDNs skip work, and why connection reuse, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and TLS 1.3 matter so much on slow mobile networks.

lessons.title: REST API design
lessons.summary: Design REST APIs that clients can guess, cache and retry safely — resources and URIs, the right verbs and status codes, RFC 9457 Problem Details errors, filtering, sorting and cursor pagination, a little HATEOAS — and implement them with ASP.NET Core minimal APIs.

lessons.title: GraphQL
lessons.summary: Understand what GraphQL really changes compared with REST — a typed schema, client-chosen fields, one round trip for nested data — and the costs it brings: server-side N+1 queries fixed with DataLoader, hard HTTP caching, and the need for depth and complexity limits.

lessons.title: gRPC
lessons.summary: Learn how gRPC works on the wire — Protocol Buffers, HTTP/2 streams, length-prefixed frames and status trailers — when to use its four call types, how deadlines and retries keep call chains healthy, why load balancing needs care, and why it is usually an internal protocol.

lessons.title: WebSockets, Server-Sent Events and long polling
lessons.summary: Push data to browsers and apps the moment it changes. Compare long polling, Server-Sent Events and WebSockets, understand why persistent connections change how you scale, and build an SSE feed, a long-poll endpoint and a SignalR hub with a replay buffer, heartbeats and reconnection in ASP.NET Core.

lessons.title: Webhooks
lessons.summary: Let one system tell another "something happened" by calling its URL. Learn to sign webhooks with HMAC and verify them in C#, block replays with timestamps, retry with backoff and jitter, make receivers idempotent, and keep delivery logs that answer "did you send it?".

lessons.title: Synchronous versus asynchronous communication
lessons.summary: Decide, for each interaction between services, whether the caller should wait for an answer. Learn temporal coupling, how latency and availability compound through synchronous chains, what asynchronous messaging really costs, and a checklist for choosing per interaction.

lessons.title: API gateways, reverse proxies and load balancers
lessons.summary: Tell apart the three boxes that sit in front of your services. Learn what reverse proxies, L4 and L7 load balancers and API gateways each do, where to terminate TLS, how forwarded headers work in ASP.NET Core, how YARP builds a gateway in .NET, and which gateway responsibilities turn into anti-patterns.

lessons.title: Service discovery
lessons.summary: When instances come and go every few minutes, callers need a live answer to "where is the orders service right now?". Learn DNS-based discovery and its caching traps, service registries with leases and heartbeats, client-side versus server-side discovery, health checks that do not flap, and how Kubernetes Services do it for you.

lessons.title: Idempotency keys
lessons.summary: Make "try again" safe. Learn how an Idempotency-Key header, a request fingerprint and a small shared store let clients retry a payment or an order without creating it twice, and build the ASP.NET Core endpoint filter that does it.

lessons.title: Rate limiting algorithms
lessons.summary: Decide how many requests each caller may make, and what happens to the rest. Compare fixed window, sliding log, sliding window counter, token bucket and leaky bucket, build them in C#, and wire ASP.NET Core's rate limiter with per-key limits, 429 and Retry-After.

lessons.title: API contracts and versioning
lessons.summary: Change an API that other teams depend on without breaking them. Learn what counts as a breaking change, compare URL, header and media-type versioning, run consumer-driven contract tests, and deprecate old versions with Sunset headers and an OpenAPI document per version, all in ASP.NET Core.

lessons.title: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter
lessons.summary: Put a time limit on every remote call, retry only failures that are temporary and operations that are safe to repeat, wait longer and slightly randomly between attempts, pass the remaining time budget downstream, and cap total retries so they cannot multiply into an outage.

lessons.title: Circuit breaker
lessons.summary: Stop calling a dependency that is clearly failing, fail fast for a while so it can recover, then let a few test calls through to check. Build the closed, open and half-open state machine in C#, tune thresholds and sampling windows with numbers, and design useful fallbacks.

lessons.title: Bulkheads, fallbacks and resilience pipelines
lessons.summary: Split shared resources (connections, threads, worker pools, deployments) so one slow dependency or noisy tenant cannot sink everything, add fallbacks that keep users working, and compose timeout, retry, circuit breaker and bulkhead in the right order, knowing why each one sits where it does.

lessons.title: Distributed request correlation
lessons.summary: Follow one user action through five services, two queues and a thousand log lines. Learn how W3C Trace Context (traceparent), .NET's Activity, correlation IDs and logging scopes fit together, and how to carry them across HTTP calls and message queues in ASP.NET Core.

modules.title: High-Level Design Foundations
modules.description: A repeatable method for designing large systems.

lessons.title: How to approach an HLD problem: the 12-step framework
lessons.summary: A repeatable 12-step method for any high-level design problem, from clarifying questions to a closing summary, with a worked visitor-pass example and a minute-by-minute budget for a 45-minute interview.

lessons.title: Clarifying requirements, users and system boundaries
lessons.summary: How to turn a one-line prompt into a clear problem — who the users and actors are, what the system must do, where its boundary lies, what is out of scope — with a reusable question bank and a hospital appointment example.

lessons.title: Non-functional requirements, assumptions and constraints
lessons.summary: Turn vague words like "fast", "always up" and "never lose data" into measurable targets — p99 latency, availability percentages, durability, RPO and RTO, throughput — and separate assumptions from hard constraints.

lessons.title: Capacity estimation: RPS, peak, bandwidth and storage
lessons.summary: Back-of-the-envelope maths for system design — average and peak requests per second, read/write ratios, bandwidth, storage over time and instance counts — with worked examples, a C# estimator and exercises that have numeric answers.

lessons.title: Latency numbers and latency budgets
lessons.summary: The order-of-magnitude latencies of memory, disk, network and distance, how to split a latency target into a budget across a request path, and why tail latency and fan-out make p99 the number that matters.

lessons.title: Availability, reliability and the nines
lessons.summary: Turn "it must always be up" into numbers. Learn the downtime each extra nine buys, how availability multiplies through a chain and improves with redundancy, and why cutting repair time (MTTR) is often the cheapest way to more nines.

lessons.title: Vertical versus horizontal scaling and elasticity
lessons.summary: Learn when to buy a bigger machine (scale up) and when to add more machines (scale out), why both hit limits, how cost grows with each, and how autoscalers decide when to add and remove instances without flapping or arriving too late.

lessons.title: Stateless versus stateful services
lessons.summary: Learn what "state" really lives inside a web server, why it blocks scaling out, when sticky sessions are an acceptable stop-gap, and how to move sessions, files, jobs and ASP.NET Core data-protection keys out of the instance so any copy can serve any request.

lessons.title: Load balancing algorithms
lessons.summary: How a load balancer decides where each request goes. Compare round robin, weighted, least connections, least response time, IP hash, consistent hashing and power of two choices; understand L4 versus L7 balancing and active versus passive health checks; and implement the main algorithms in C#.

lessons.title: Caching layers in a system
lessons.summary: A request can be answered by the browser, a CDN, a reverse proxy, the app's memory, a distributed cache or the database's buffer cache before it ever touches disk. Learn what belongs in each layer, how HTTP caching headers control the outer layers, how ASP.NET Core output caching and HybridCache handle the inner ones, and how staleness and invalidation add up across layers.

lessons.title: CDN architecture
lessons.summary: How a content delivery network puts copies of your content close to users, how edge, shield and origin work together, and how to control what gets cached, for how long, and for whom.

lessons.title: DNS and traffic routing
lessons.summary: How a name like api.example.in becomes an IP address, how TTLs trade change speed for load and resilience, and how GeoDNS, latency-based routing, anycast and health-checked failover steer users to the right region.

lessons.title: Choosing and scaling the database tier
lessons.summary: A step-by-step ladder for scaling the database tier, from one well-tuned primary through pooling, replicas, caching and partitioning to sharding, and how to pick SQL or NoSQL stores from access patterns instead of fashion.

lessons.title: Object storage
lessons.summary: How object storage differs from block and file storage, and how to build uploads and downloads on it properly — presigned URLs, multipart uploads, lifecycle tiers, and keeping file metadata in the database.

lessons.title: Background processing and job queues
lessons.summary: How to move slow, unreliable and scheduled work out of the request path — in-process with BackgroundService and Channels, or durably with job queues and schedulers — and how to make jobs safe under at-least-once delivery with retries, leases and idempotency.

lessons.title: Cost estimation
lessons.summary: Turn a design into a monthly bill — compute, storage, egress, managed services and observability — compare on-demand, reserved and spot pricing, compute cost per request, and build a C# cost calculator whose unit prices are explicit, dated assumptions.

lessons.title: Explaining trade-offs and failure scenarios
lessons.summary: How to argue a design — consistency versus availability, latency versus cost, simplicity versus flexibility — with per-operation decisions, failure-mode tables, a trade-off statement template, and C# code that serves stale reads but refuses unsafe writes.

modules.title: Caching, Messaging and Asynchronous Processing
modules.description: Make systems fast and decoupled without losing data.

lessons.title: Why caching works
lessons.summary: A cache works because real traffic keeps asking for the same small set of things. Learn locality, hot sets and Zipf-shaped traffic, the hit-ratio arithmetic that predicts latency and database load, and how to tell when a cache is not worth its cost.

lessons.title: Cache-aside, read-through, write-through and write-behind
lessons.summary: The five ways an application, a cache and a database can share the work of reading and writing data. Learn each flow, what happens when one part fails, and how to build them in ASP.NET Core behind a small cache abstraction.

lessons.title: Cache invalidation, TTL and eviction policies
lessons.summary: How cached data leaves the cache — by expiring (TTL), by being invalidated when the source changes, or by being evicted when memory is full. Build an LRU cache in C#, use versioned keys and change events, and calculate how long users can see stale data.

lessons.title: Redis data structures and use cases
lessons.summary: Redis is an in-memory server for data structures, not just a key-value cache. Learn strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams and pub/sub with the problems each one solves, plus TTLs, persistence (RDB and AOF), the single-threaded model and cluster hash slots.

lessons.title: Cache stampede, penetration and hot keys
lessons.summary: The five ways a cache turns from a speed boost into an outage — stampedes, penetration, hot keys, avalanches and the cache itself going down — and the defences for each, from request coalescing and Bloom filters to TTL jitter, local hot-key caches and safe fallback to the database.

lessons.title: Message queues
lessons.summary: A message queue is a durable waiting line between the code that creates work (producers) and the code that does it (consumers). It absorbs bursts, lets each side scale and fail independently, and uses acknowledgements so that work is not lost when a consumer crashes.

lessons.title: RabbitMQ exchanges and routing
lessons.summary: In RabbitMQ, producers publish to exchanges, not queues. Bindings decide which queues get a copy (direct, topic, fanout or headers routing). Prefetch, manual acks, quorum queues and publisher confirms decide how fast and how safely messages flow.

lessons.title: Kafka topics, partitions and consumer groups
lessons.summary: Kafka is a replicated, partitioned, append-only log. Producers append records to partitions chosen by key; consumer groups read at their own offsets, so many independent consumers can read the same data, replay it, and scale up to one consumer per partition, with ordering guaranteed only within a partition.

lessons.title: Delivery guarantees
lessons.summary: Every messaging system chooses between losing messages (at-most-once) and duplicating them (at-least-once). Exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network is not achievable in general; exactly-once effect ("effectively-once") is, by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent, transactional processing.

lessons.title: Idempotent consumers and inbox deduplication
lessons.summary: Because brokers deliver at least once, every consumer must make a second delivery harmless. Use naturally idempotent writes where you can, and otherwise record a stable message id or business key in an inbox table with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the effect. For external side effects, pass an idempotency key and record intent before the call.

lessons.title: Retries and dead-letter queues
lessons.summary: When a message cannot be processed, retry it later with growing delays for temporary problems, move it to a dead-letter queue when retrying cannot help, alert a human, and replay it safely once the cause is fixed.

lessons.title: Transactional outbox
lessons.summary: Save the business change and the event that announces it in the same database transaction, then let a separate relay publish the event, so a crash can never leave the database and the message broker disagreeing.

lessons.title: Messaging patterns catalogue
lessons.summary: A working catalogue of the messaging patterns you will meet in real systems, from point-to-point and publish-subscribe to claim check, scatter-gather and the resequencer, with a diagram, a C# sketch and a "use it when" rule for each.

lessons.title: Eventual consistency
lessons.summary: Learn what "eventually consistent" really promises, how to measure and budget the lag, how to design screens that stay honest while data catches up, how to give users their own writes back immediately, and how to resolve conflicts when two copies disagree.

lessons.title: Sagas and compensating transactions
lessons.summary: Run a business process that spans several services as a chain of local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes its business effect, and coordinate it with an orchestrator or by events, with idempotent steps and explicit timeouts.

modules.title: Distributed Systems
modules.description: Why distributed systems fail, and the tools for living with it.

lessons.title: Why distributed systems are difficult
lessons.summary: Once a job runs on more than one computer, messages get lost, nodes go quiet without dying, and a timeout cannot tell you whether the work happened. This lesson shows why, and how to design for it.

lessons.title: Clock skew, ordering and logical clocks
lessons.summary: Every machine's clock is a little wrong, so timestamps cannot reliably say which event came first. Learn how much clocks drift, what NTP can and cannot fix, and how Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks order events correctly.

lessons.title: CAP theorem and PACELC, properly interpreted
lessons.summary: CAP says that during a network partition a replicated system must choose between answering every request and always returning the latest data. PACELC adds the everyday choice between low latency and consistency when there is no partition. Learn what the theorem actually says, and what it doesn't.

lessons.title: Consistency models
lessons.summary: A consistency model is a promise about what a read can return when data has several copies. Learn linearizable, sequential, causal, read-your-writes, monotonic reads and eventual consistency, the anomaly each one allows, and how to build the session guarantees most apps actually need.

lessons.title: Replication and leader-follower
lessons.summary: Replication keeps copies of your data on several machines. Learn how leader-follower replication works with synchronous, asynchronous and semi-synchronous commits, what replication lag does to your users, how failover loses data or causes split-brain, and when multi-leader or leaderless designs make sense.

lessons.title: Quorums
lessons.summary: Keep N copies of every item and ask only some of them on each read and write. If the readers and writers you ask always overlap (R + W > N), a read sees the latest acknowledged write. Learn where that promise holds, where sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and clock-based versions quietly break it, and how read repair heals stale copies.

lessons.title: Consensus fundamentals (Raft)
lessons.summary: Consensus lets a group of machines agree on one ordered log of decisions even when some of them crash. Learn how Raft does it with terms, elections, log replication and a commit index, model leader election in C#, see where homemade versions break, and why you should almost always use etcd or ZooKeeper instead of writing your own.

lessons.title: Distributed locks and fencing tokens
lessons.summary: A distributed lock is really a lease, a lock that expires, and any process holding one can pause long enough for it to expire without noticing. Learn why leases alone are unsafe, how fencing tokens make the protected resource reject stale holders, how Redis locks and the Redlock debate fit in, and when a PostgreSQL advisory lock is all you need.

lessons.title: Split-brain and failure detection
lessons.summary: Automatic failover needs to decide that a node is dead, and in a distributed system that decision can be wrong. When it is, two nodes both act as primary (split-brain) and data diverges. Learn how heartbeats and phi accrual detectors trade detection speed for false alarms, and how quorum fencing, STONITH and self-fencing make a wrong suspicion harmless.

lessons.title: Sharding, hot partitions and consistent hashing
lessons.summary: When one database node cannot hold all the data or absorb all the writes, you split the data into shards by a key. Learn how to choose that key, why modulo hashing moves almost everything when you add a node, how consistent hashing with virtual nodes moves only a fair share, how hot partitions defeat even perfect hashing, and how to reshard a live system without losing writes.

lessons.title: Distributed transactions and two-phase commit
lessons.summary: How two-phase commit makes several databases commit or abort together, why it blocks when the coordinator fails, how XA and PostgreSQL prepared transactions expose it, and why sagas are usually the better choice across services.

lessons.title: Backpressure, load shedding and graceful degradation
lessons.summary: What to do when work arrives faster than you can finish it — bounded queues that push back, admission control that sheds the right requests early, and brownouts that switch off optional features so the core keeps working.

lessons.title: Retry storms and resilience engineering
lessons.summary: How well-meant retries multiply across layers into a storm that keeps a system down after the original fault is gone, and the tools that stop it — retrying at one layer, retry budgets, jittered backoff, deadlines, "don't retry" signals and circuit breakers.

lessons.title: Concurrency patterns
lessons.summary: The core patterns for doing many things at once safely in .NET — producer-consumer with Channels, the thread pool, async/await pitfalls, actors, locks, semaphores, immutable snapshots, Interlocked and CAS, futures and fork-join — with when to use each and how each one fails.

modules.title: Security, Reliability and Observability
modules.description: Secure, measurable, recoverable systems.

lessons.title: Authentication versus authorization
lessons.summary: Authentication answers "who are you?" and authorization answers "are you allowed to do this?". Learn the difference, how credentials become an identity, sessions versus tokens, when to return 401 versus 403, and the mistakes that cause most access-control breaches.

lessons.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
lessons.summary: OAuth 2.0 lets an app act on a user's behalf without seeing their password. OpenID Connect adds a standard way to log the user in. Learn the four roles, authorization code with PKCE, client credentials, refresh tokens and rotation, scopes versus claims, ID tokens versus access tokens, and how to wire it all up in ASP.NET Core.

lessons.title: JWT validation and limitations
lessons.summary: A JWT is a signed, base64url-encoded set of claims that any server holding the right key can check without a database call. Learn its structure, HS256 versus RS256 and ES256, the full validation checklist (signature, alg, kid, iss, aud, exp, nbf), the attacks that skipped steps allow, and its real limits around revocation and size. Then build HS256 signing and a validator in C#.

lessons.title: Role-based and policy-based authorization
lessons.summary: Roles answer "what kind of user is this?", policies answer "may this user do this action on this resource right now?". Learn RBAC, ABAC/PBAC and relationship-based models, ASP.NET Core policies, requirements and handlers, resource-based authorization and ownership checks, and how to keep permission data fast and correct at scale.

lessons.title: Secure password storage and secret management
lessons.summary: Store passwords so that a stolen database doesn't reveal them, and keep the application's own secrets (connection strings, API keys, signing keys) out of code and rotatable. Learn salts, slow hashes (PBKDF2, bcrypt, Argon2), peppers, constant-time comparison, upgrade-on-login, and secret management with user secrets, environment variables, Azure Key Vault and managed identities.

lessons.title: TLS and encryption at rest
lessons.summary: Protect data while it travels (TLS, certificates, HSTS, mutual TLS) and while it sits on disk (disk and database encryption, column-level AES-GCM, envelope encryption with a key service), and know which threat each layer actually stops.

lessons.title: SQL injection, XSS, CSRF and SSRF
lessons.summary: Learn the four classic web attacks (SQL injection, cross-site scripting, cross-site request forgery and server-side request forgery) as one idea, untrusted data crossing into a place where it is treated as code or authority, and fix each one in ASP.NET Core with parameters, encoding, antiforgery tokens and outbound allow-lists.

lessons.title: Least privilege and audit trails
lessons.summary: Give every person, service and token only the access its job needs (PostgreSQL roles and column grants, managed identities, narrowly scoped short-lived tokens), and record who did what in an audit trail that is complete, free of secrets, tamper-evident through hash chaining, and kept for as long as the rules require.

lessons.title: Multi-tenant security
lessons.summary: Keep one customer's data invisible to every other customer in a shared platform by choosing an isolation model, enforcing it in PostgreSQL with row-level security (and knowing its traps), carrying the tenant context through every request, job, cache and log, and proving it with automated cross-tenant leak tests.

lessons.title: SLI, SLO, SLA and error budgets
lessons.summary: Measure reliability the way users feel it (SLIs as good events over valid events), set targets that are high enough but not perfect (SLOs), keep contractual promises looser than internal targets (SLAs), and use the gap, the error budget, to decide when to ship features and when to fix reliability, with burn-rate alerts that page only when the budget is really at risk.

lessons.title: Logs, metrics, traces and OpenTelemetry
lessons.summary: How to see inside a running system. Structured logs, RED and USE metrics, and distributed traces, produced in .NET with ILogger, System.Diagnostics.Metrics and ActivitySource, shipped with OpenTelemetry over OTLP, without letting cardinality or volume blow up your bill.

lessons.title: Alerting and incident response
lessons.summary: Page people only when users are hurting and a human can help. Alert on symptoms with SLO burn rates, route the rest to tickets, run incidents with clear roles and runbooks, and learn from them with blameless postmortems. Includes a failure simulation lab built from real-looking logs, traces and metrics.

lessons.title: Backups, disaster recovery, RTO and RPO
lessons.summary: Decide how much data you can afford to lose (RPO) and how long you can be down (RTO), then build backups and DR that meet those numbers. Covers full, incremental and logical backups, PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery with WAL archiving, restore drills, DR tiers and what each one costs.

lessons.title: Chaos engineering
lessons.summary: Break your system on purpose, in small controlled ways, to find weaknesses before your users do. Write a steady-state hypothesis, limit the blast radius, set abort conditions, inject faults with ASP.NET Core middleware and HttpClient handlers, and run game days that test people and runbooks as well as code.

modules.title: Deployment, Infrastructure and Cloud Architecture
modules.description: From laptop to production.

lessons.title: Development, testing, staging and production
lessons.summary: Why software runs in several copies (development, test, staging, production), how close those copies must be to each other, how ASP.NET Core picks configuration per environment, and how to use realistic data outside production without leaking real people's details or sending them real messages.

lessons.title: Docker, Dockerfiles and Docker Compose
lessons.summary: What containers and images really are, how to write a small, non-root, multi-stage Dockerfile for an ASP.NET Core API, how layer caching makes builds fast, and how Docker Compose runs the API with PostgreSQL, Redis and RabbitMQ locally, with health checks and graceful shutdown in the app.

lessons.title: CI/CD with GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps
lessons.summary: How a commit becomes a tested, versioned artifact and then a production release, using GitHub Actions and Azure Pipelines YAML, with service containers for integration tests, immutable artifacts promoted by digest, environments with approvals, OIDC instead of stored cloud keys, and app-side version and smoke-test support in ASP.NET Core.

lessons.title: Reverse proxies and IIS hosting for ASP.NET Core
lessons.summary: What a reverse proxy does in front of Kestrel, how IIS hosts ASP.NET Core through the ASP.NET Core Module in-process or out-of-process, what web.config controls, how Nginx and YARP compare, and how to configure forwarded headers so the app sees the real client IP and scheme without trusting spoofed headers.

lessons.title: Azure App Service, Container Apps and AKS
lessons.summary: Choose between Azure App Service, Azure Container Apps and Azure Kubernetes Service by comparing what you hand over to Azure, how each one scales, and what drives its bill. Then make an ASP.NET Core app behave well on any of them with health probes, forwarded headers, configuration from environment variables and graceful shutdown, all testable locally with Docker.

lessons.title: Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Cache for Redis, Service Bus and Blob Storage
lessons.summary: What Azure's managed PostgreSQL, Redis, Service Bus and Blob Storage actually do for you, which tier gives which guarantee, how high availability and failover behave, and how to run free local equivalents in Docker. The C# side shows options validation, token-based (managed identity) connections, dependency health checks and testable abstractions.

lessons.title: Azure API Management
lessons.summary: What Azure API Management adds in front of your APIs (products, subscriptions, a policy pipeline, versions, revisions and a developer portal), how to write rate-limit, quota, JWT validation and transformation policies, how the backend ASP.NET Core app should cooperate with the gateway, and how a YARP gateway in Docker gives you a free local alternative.

lessons.title: Infrastructure as Code
lessons.summary: Describe servers, databases, networks and secrets as reviewed code instead of portal clicks, using Bicep and Terraform (shown as text); understand state, plan and what-if, drift and how to detect it, modules and per-environment parameters; run a real Terraform workflow for free with the Docker provider; and make the ASP.NET Core app fail fast when its infrastructure wiring is wrong.

lessons.title: Kubernetes fundamentals and autoscaling
lessons.summary: What Kubernetes actually does for an ASP.NET Core service, explained from the ground up. Covers pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, liveness, readiness and startup probes, CPU and memory requests and limits, and how the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler decides how many replicas to run, with the arithmetic and the failure modes.

lessons.title: Blue-green, canary and rolling deployments
lessons.summary: How to ship a new version without betting the whole user base on it. Compares rolling, blue-green and canary deployments by risk, cost and rollback speed, explains traffic shifting and feature flags, and builds an automated canary analyzer in C# that compares error rates between the old and new versions.

lessons.title: Database migrations during deployments
lessons.summary: How to change a PostgreSQL schema while several versions of an ASP.NET Core app run at once during rolling, blue-green and canary deployments; where migrations should run (pipeline step, job, never every pod at start-up), how EF Core bundles and idempotent scripts fit, how to keep each step backward compatible, avoid lock queues, dual-write with triggers, and roll forward safely.

lessons.title: Cost monitoring and infrastructure reliability
lessons.summary: How to see, explain and control cloud spend (tags, budgets with actual and forecast alerts, cost exports, unit economics, shared-cost allocation, right-sizing, reservations, non-production schedules), how to spot cost anomalies with a robust C# detector, and how to trade reliability against cost with SLOs, availability arithmetic and zone redundancy, with Docker-based and open-source alternatives that need no paid cloud.

modules.title: Advanced Architecture Patterns
modules.description: Big-system patterns, the problems they solve, and what they cost.

lessons.title: Modular monolith versus microservices
